How this feed is made

Underneath it is a database of daily price history for several thousand companies listed on the NASDAQ and NYSE, going back years. Those companies are organised two ways at once: by the public sector and industry classifications everyone uses, and by hand — into roughly 250 groups drawn from news reports, podcasts and industry deep dives, which cut across the official taxonomy in ways it never would. Layered on top are forward analyst projections and the transcripts of recent earnings calls. Holding all of it in one place is the point: it means every brief is grounded in primary, verifiable data — prices as the exchange reported them, fundamentals drawn from company filings, and what management actually said on the call — rather than in whatever a search happens to surface. Where the database cannot answer a question, the agents do search the web — with a blocklist that strips out sites publishing volume rather than insight, and a standing instruction to prefer primary sources and filings, or to drop a fact rather than source it badly.

The newsroom. Three automated agents run in sequence, imitating how a real desk works:

  1. The Hypothesizer reads a daily snapshot of what moved and what changed direction, and proposes one question worth chasing.
  2. The Investigator goes and checks — querying the price database, reading company fundamentals and research notes, and searching the web — then reports back with evidence.
  3. The Editor scores that evidence. Weak stories are spiked; strong ones are written up as the article you are reading.

The Editor is instructed to observe, never to advise — so you will not find buy or sell calls here.

Chilean Inflation Sets Santander Chile's Margin, and the Bank Expects Less Next Year

Hypothesis Opus 5 · Research Opus 5 · Writing Opus 5 · Prompt v1.7

Chile's central bank has not moved the policy rate since July, yet Santander Chile's quarterly profit swung from a 40% year-on-year gain in the second quarter to a 4.2% decline in the third. The variable doing the work is the inflation adjustment on a disclosed net gap of CLP 7.9tn in indexed instruments, which the bank enlarged in the second quarter to capture the inflation rebound and then cut.

That makes the margin a function of Chilean consumer prices, and management has told investors to expect less of them: 2027 guidance assumes 3.1% indexed inflation, with return on equity of 22-24% against more than 24% this year. Banco de Chile quantifies the same lever at CLP 91.1bn of net financial income per 100 basis points of inflation and sees roughly 20 basis points of margin going away.

Both carry the regional group's richest book multiples, 3.16x and 3.37x against Itaú Unibanco's 2.25x, into a headwind they forecast themselves.

Santander Chile's third-quarter profit fell by well over a third from the second quarter, and Chile's central bank never touched the policy rate. The lender, a Santiago retail, middle-market and corporate bank majority-owned by Spain's Santander, earned CLP 237.1bn in the quarter against CLP 382.6bn in the one before, and the drop was 4.2% measured against a year earlier.

The quarter was read in New York as deterioration in a bank whose returns had been among the best in Latin America. It was something narrower. The policy rate has sat at 4.50% since well before the unanimous October hold, the fifth-plus consecutive meeting without a change. What moved was the inflation adjustment: the variation in Chile's unidad de fomento, the inflation-indexed accounting unit that reprices a large slice of Chilean bank assets, dropped from 2.46% in the second quarter to 0.58% in the third, and net interest and readjustment income fell 18.1% sequentially with it.

The CLP 7.9tn line that moves the quarter

The size of the lever is disclosed. Santander Chile reported a net gap in inflation-indexed instruments of CLP 7,906,527m at the end of September, against an interest-earning asset yield of 7.6%, cost of funds of 3.8% and a year-to-date net interest margin of 4.1%. The bank does not hold that position passively: it widened the gap during the second-quarter inflation rebound to capture the higher print, then reduced it in the third.

Underneath the inflation trade sits the part of the franchise that does not depend on a price index. Year-to-date efficiency was 33%, an improvement of 290 basis points on a year earlier, and deposits grew 9% year to date against loan growth of 3.9%. "I think the first position in the Chilean industry is still safely on our side," Cristian Vicuña, head of strategy and investor relations, told investors on November 4.

Management's own 2027 assumptions are where the mechanism turns. The bank guided to 3.1% indexed inflation, a flat 4.5% policy rate, net interest margin of about 4.0% and return on equity of 22-24%, below the more than 24% it expects for 2026. Consensus still models 2027 earnings growth of 4.3%. The macro backdrop it guides into is thin: "Mining fell to its lowest level since 1996 in August due to lower ore grades, maintenance, and weather," chief economist Andrés Sansone said on the same call, with mining output now expected to contract 6% to 8% this year.

Banco de Chile holds the same lever and a worse consumer book

Banco de Chile, the 1893-founded commercial bank that is the country's other large listed lender, puts a number on it directly: 100 basis points of inflation is worth CLP 91.1bn of net financial income, while 100 basis points of interest rates moves margin by only about 30 basis points, and only after roughly three years of full repricing. Its readjustment income contracted 64.6% in the third quarter; third-quarter net income was 1.8% below a year earlier on revenue up 8.8%. It guides 2026 inflation at 4.7% falling to 3% in 2027, an effect it sizes at roughly 20 basis points of margin.

It also has the weaker credit trend of the two, with credit losses up 21.2% year on year on retail delinquency, even though its 0.96% third-quarter cost of risk remains well inside Santander Chile's 1.4% year to date. Yet Banco de Chile carries the higher valuation on the lower return: 3.37x trailing book against Santander Chile's 3.16x, with full-year return on average capital and reserves guided to 22%. Both sit above Itaú Unibanco at 2.25x and Credicorp at 2.51x.

Twelve months in pesos, twelve months in dollars

In Santiago, nothing has broken. Santander Chile's local shares rose 19.1% over twelve months and Banco de Chile's 10.8%. The American depositary receipts returned 7.1% and 0.3% over the same dates, a gap of roughly ten percentage points that is the peso, which closed at 1,038 per dollar on November 27 after copper fell 21.5% from its September peak. The dollar proxy for the whole market, the iShares MSCI Chile ETF, fell 8.7%.

So the flat dollar year is currency, and the earnings record contradicts it: Santander Chile's year-to-date return on equity was 24.5%. The three-month slide in both receipts, however, has a genuine companion in the accounts, because the third quarter is the first in which the indexed adjustment worked against the margin rather than for it. What has not happened is any de-rating in pesos. Investors are paying the regional set's richest book multiples for returns that both managements expect to be lower next year, for a reason neither bank controls.

Chile's central bank projects headline inflation back near 3% by the second quarter of 2027, which is target achieved for the country and a shrinking revenue line for its two largest listed lenders. Every quarter from here, the number that decides how much these banks earn will be published by the statistics office before either of them reports.

The setup

Where it standsBoth banks' third-quarter profits fell year on year as indexed inflation reset, while local Santiago shares still hold twelve-month gains the dollar receipts do not.
Would confirmIndexed inflation near the guided 3.1% for 2027, Santander Chile net interest margin at or below 4.0%, Banco de Chile margin down about 20 basis points.
Would invalidateChilean inflation holding above 4% into 2027, Santander Chile return on equity sustained above 24%, or Banco de Chile cost of risk back below 0.9%.
Watch nextSantander Chile's fourth quarter carries a roughly CLP 40bn non-cash deferred-tax charge from Chile's corporate rate cut to 25.5% in 2027.
ValuationSantander Chile 14.3x trailing earnings and 3.16x book; Banco de Chile 16.2x and 3.37x, against Itaú Unibanco 2.25x and Credicorp 2.51x book.

Millicom Paid $99m to Settle With Four Ex-Guatemala Executives, Halving Quarterly Profit

Hypothesis Opus 5 · Research Opus 5 · Writing Opus 5 · Prompt v1.7

Millicom's third quarter reads as decay in exactly one line and as a record in every other, and the share price has sided with the one line. Profit attributable to shareholders fell to $98m from $195m, almost entirely because the company booked a $99m settlement with four former executives of its Guatemalan business and $20m of Colombian integration severance.

Underneath, adjusted earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortization set a quarterly record of $1.1bn, up 7.7% organically, net leverage fell to 2.53x, and Colombia — now the group's largest market, bigger than Guatemala — posted its best-ever margin at 44.2%.

The operating record does not explain a fall of nearly a quarter from August. What might: América Móvil's Claro grew faster than Tigo in both core markets, and on 6.87x enterprise value to EBITDA against Claro's parent at 5.36x, Millicom is not the cheap one.

Millicom International Cellular, which sells mobile service, fixed broadband and mobile money under the Tigo brand in ten Latin American markets, halved its third-quarter profit by settling with four men who used to run its Guatemalan business. Profit attributable to shareholders came in at $98m against $195m a year earlier, and earnings of $0.58 a share missed what analysts expected by more than 40%. Nearly every operating line in the same quarter set a record.

The stock has been held as a Central American dollar annuity carrying a risky Colombian acquisition. The filings describe the reverse arrangement. Colombia, bought from Telefónica this year, is now the largest market in the group at $908m of quarterly service revenue, roughly 2.3 times Guatemala's $392m, and only three of the ten markets — Panama, El Salvador and Ecuador — use the dollar at all. Guatemala transacts in quetzales, Honduras in lempiras.

What the $99m bought

The charge sits in other non-operating expenses: $99m for settlement agreements with four former executives of Tigo Guatemala, of which $31m was paid in the quarter and $68m remains payable over seven years. It resolved all pending material litigation and claims involving those parties, which management called the removal of a significant source of financial and regulatory uncertainty. The concentrated country risk in this business is fiscal rather than currency: at the end of September the estimated tax risk exposure of Millicom's subsidiaries stood at $378m, against $60m of provisions recorded.

The Colombian book earned its best margin while being absorbed

Colombian service revenue grew 7.5% organically and adjusted EBITDA of $417m landed at a 44.2% margin, the highest Millicom has recorded there, while the quarter still carried $20m of integration severance. The Tigo brand consolidation in Colombia took effect on 14 October.

"Following the acquisition of Coltel, our teams moved quickly to integrate operations, simplify our business, improve efficiencies and implement our commercial strategy," chief financial officer Bart Vanhaeren told investors on 5 November, describing the result as "bringing up the acquired lower-margin business from Coltel to our highest EBITDA margin in Colombia ever despite still incurring integration costs." Net leverage fell to 2.53x including Colombia, Ecuador and Uruguay, inside the sub-2.5x year-end path, and the $3.00 annual dividend stayed in four equal installments.

Growth comes from re-pricing the prepaid base

What one Tigo customer pays rose about a fifth: group mobile monthly revenue per user reached $7.4 from $6.2. The engine is migration, not new SIM cards. Postpaid net additions of 390,000 took that base to 17.2m, and 73% of postpaid gross sales came from existing prepaid users, a conversion rate of 87% in Guatemala.

Two lines went the other way. Millicom lost 86,000 home customers sequentially, attributed about one-third to the Colombian earthquake and two-thirds to deliberate pricing, and business-to-business revenue of $404m grew only 2.1% organically as large government projects in Medellín and Panama rolled off, with further roll-off flagged for the fourth quarter.

The decline belongs to Millicom alone

The shares have fallen 14.9% over three months and 23.8% from a closing high of $104.31 on 6 August, with the downtrend dating from 5 November, the day results landed. One session, 12 November, took 9.6% on 4.8m shares, roughly six times the prior month's daily average, a week after results and two days after a UBS upgrade. Over the same three months Liberty Latin America rose 14.0%, TIM Brasil 16.5% and América Móvil 6.9%.

So the operating record accounts for almost none of the fall, and the settlement accounts for the earnings line without touching cash generation: equity free cash flow rose 27% to $316m, with roughly $870m banked against about $1.1bn guided for the year. What the price may instead be discounting is share. In the same quarter América Móvil's Claro grew Central American service revenue 11.4% and the region's EBITDA 16.1%, and Colombian postpaid service revenue 12%, ahead of Tigo's 6.5% in Guatemala and 7.5% in Colombia. Nor is Millicom the discounted asset of the group: at 6.87x trailing enterprise value to EBITDA it is dearer than América Móvil at 5.36x, and the case for the fall being an error rests on the one-off charges not recurring — against next year's consensus earnings of $6.80 a share, the stock stands near 11.7x by our arithmetic, versus 21.1x on this year's charge-depressed base.

The largest holder is not waiting for that argument to settle. Xavier Niel's Atlas Investissement owns 49.5% of the shares outstanding excluding treasury and entered a derivative on 24 November for up to 1,677,459 more — settlement conditional on regulatory clearances and on Millicom confirming that crossing half the company would not accelerate any of its material debt.

The setup

Where it standsShares are 23.8% below their 6 August high after a quarter of record adjusted EBITDA, improved leverage and a halved reported profit.
Would confirmColombian EBITDA margin holding near 44% in the fourth quarter and full-year equity free cash flow landing near the $1.1bn guided.
Would invalidateGuatemalan or Colombian organic service revenue growth staying below Claro's, or net leverage rising back above 2.5x.
Watch nextFourth-quarter results, where management has flagged further business-to-business project roll-off, and the $0.75 dividend installment due around 15 January 2027.
Valuation6.87x trailing enterprise value to EBITDA against América Móvil's 5.36x; near 11.7x next year's $6.80 consensus earnings versus 21.1x on this year's charge-hit base.

Originating hypothesis

single ticker band breakdown dollarized arpu vs peso integration mechanics · subject: TIGO

Millicom is the one Latin American carrier on this shelf still breaking down rather than repairing, and the one the Desk has never examined as a business — TIGO has stepped strongly bullish to strongly bearish across the 90-, 180- and 365-day windows and mildly bearish to strongly bearish inside 30 days, with no appearance in any 1-month, 3-month, 6-month or 12-month mover list, so this is a gradual year-long de-rating rather than a pop — and rather than another regional-discount or price-versus-business divergence (the shape already run on Liberty Latin America, América Móvil and TIM Brasil, where Millicom appeared only as a trend-band mention and none of its own numbers were load-bearing), the question is a what-does-one-Tigo-customer-actually-pay-and-in-what-currency question told end to end for one company: Millicom earns the majority of its service revenue in fully dollarized Guatemala, Honduras, Panama, El Salvador and Costa Rica, markets where it bought out its Comcel partners to reach full ownership and where mobile is overwhelmingly prepaid, so the revenue line carries no FX translation at all but does carry concentrated regulatory and tax exposure the "LatAm" label conceals, bolted onto a Colombian fixed-and-mobile book priced in pesos that it has just enlarged by absorbing Telefónica's Colombian operation, financed with dollar debt against a stated leverage target and an equity-free-cash-flow figure management uses to size buybacks and its reinstated dividend, with towers and spectrum partly sold or leased back — so the thing to settle is whether the dollarized Central American cash annuity, the Colombian integration or the balance sheet is what actually deteriorated.

El Niño Rain Lifted Klabin's Cost Per Tonne 12% as Suzano Cut Its Own and Raised Prices

Hypothesis Opus 5 · Research Opus 5 · Writing Opus 5 · Prompt v1.7

Two Brazilian eucalyptus producers reported three business days apart, and the wood in the ground separated them. Klabin's total cash cost per tonne sold rose to R$3,483 as El Niño rainfall disrupted forestry and forced purchases of standing timber, and its adjusted EBITDA margin narrowed six points to 33%. Suzano's pulp production cash cost fell 2% sequentially to R$825 a tonne while realized pulp fetched $591.

The two cost measures are not identical and their levels do not compare, but their slopes do, and the shares followed: Suzano up 8% in dollars over the past month, Klabin down 10% in reais, against an Ibovespa that moved 0.5%. The awkward part is that Klabin's price gain came from export pulp rather than from the contracted Brazilian packaging book meant to insulate it.

Klabin and Suzano both grow eucalyptus in Brazil, and both told investors this month what a tonne of it now costs them. The answers moved in opposite directions. Klabin's total cash cost per tonne sold, including scheduled maintenance downtime, rose 12% year on year to R$3,483, of which the company attributed about R$111 to extraordinary weather and geopolitical pressure. Suzano's pulp production cash cost ex-downtime fell 2% sequentially to R$825. The two numbers measure different things — one an integrated pulp, paper and conversion book, the other a pulp mill — so the level does not compare. The slope does.

Until these results the market treated both as hard-currency assets grown in Brazil. On the 26 October session when the Ibovespa fell 13.88%, Suzano's American depositary shares rose 2.1% and Klabin rose 3.2%, both on roughly four times normal volume. What the quarters showed is that only one of them is being paid for fibre on improving terms, and that Klabin's insulation from the pulp cycle works in both directions.

Rain in the plantations, not weakness in the boxes

Klabin's revenue rose 3% to R$5.57bn, yet adjusted EBITDA fell 12% to R$1.856bn and the margin dropped to 33% from 39%. The cause was physical: rainfall tied to El Niño disrupted forestry operations and forced higher wood inventories and purchases of standing timber, with chief executive Cristiano Teixeira saying the extra costs should mostly phase out by the second quarter of 2027.

Where the revenue came from matters more. Klabin's pulp line grew 6% to R$1.51bn on an 18% rise in dollar short-fibre prices, while corrugated-box revenue of R$1.7bn was flat because implemented price increases exactly offset a 2% volume decline to 245 thousand tonnes. More than 70% of the packaging area is contracted with brands including JBS, Nestlé, Unilever and Natura, and Brazilian corrugated shipments are forecast up only 1.6% to 2.0% this year. A contracted book in a 2% market defends price and delivers no growth.

It also carries R$24bn of net debt at 3.3x adjusted EBITDA, financed into a policy rate the central bank held at 13.75% on 4 November after five consecutive cuts. Below-the-line financing costs consumed most of the quarter's operating profit, and management says the end of the investment cycle should support deleveraging from 2027. On 6 August, a quarter before the cost miss, Teixeira told investors: "for the next quarters, you're going to see a significant free cash flow generation in the company." The trailing free-cash-flow yield is 2.5%, and the shares carry 6.09x trailing EV/EBITDA and 2.15x book.

Suzano announced a price and collected it

Suzano's pulp segment earned R$4.8bn of EBITDA at a 50% margin on 3.19m tonnes at $591 a tonne. At the post-election rate near R$5.60 to the dollar that realization is roughly R$3,310 a tonne against R$825 of production cash cost. Two $20-a-tonne Asian increases landed, the second effective 11 November, after consultancies counted more than 900,000 tonnes of bleached chemical pulp pulled from the market mid-quarter.

"We confirm that during October, our price increase announcements were fully implemented with no concessions," pulp vice-president Leonardo Grimaldi said on 6 November, adding that Chinese order intake showed "no decrease at all."

The counterweights are real. Chinese hardwood spot in Shandong averaged 4,613.33 RMB a tonne on 20 November, up 0.51% in five days and still near the lows even as imports rose 23% month on month. Suzano lifted full-year cash cost guidance from R$800 to R$825 a tonne because Brent ran $91 to $98 against a planning assumption of $84. Buying Kimberly-Clark's stake in the Arbex consumer business pushed net debt to R$76.3bn, US$14.7bn, and leverage to 3.7x, while Arbex's 16% margin helped compress consolidated gross margin to 23.7% from 30.4%. Suzano guides net debt below US$14bn by year-end on seasonal fourth-quarter cash flow, and chief executive João Fernandez de Abreu said on 6 November that after Arbex, "nothing else is on our agenda at the moment."

What the split actually rests on

Cerrado is no longer the variable: the 2.55m-tonne mill hit nameplate within months of its 2024 start-up and should run near 2.57m tonnes this year. What moved in Suzano's favor was other producers' downtime and a competitor's Indonesian delay, conditions it does not control, met by a cost line it does. Klabin's position is the mirror image: a price book that worked and a forest that did not.

That accounts for most of the 18-point gap between the two shares over the past month, and it is why the cheaper of the two on every currency-consistent anchor is the one that rose. Suzano trades at 5.39x trailing EV/EBITDA and a 9.1% free-cash-flow yield against Klabin's 6.09x and 2.5%. Forward earnings multiples on both are unusable, dividing dollar or five-share unit prices by reais per-share estimates.

Klabin expects the rain premium out of its cost line by the second quarter of 2027. Later the same year Arauco's Sucuriú mill in Mato Grosso do Sul is guided to start up, carrying more new short-fibre capacity in a single plant than Suzano's Cerrado added, and returning both Brazilian producers to the question neither can settle on its own: what a tonne is worth in China.

The setup

Where it standsSuzano's pulp cost per tonne is falling with two implemented price increases; Klabin's cost per tonne is up 12% on weather with flat box volumes.
Would confirmSuzano holding realized pulp near $591 a tonne with cash cost at or below R$825, while Klabin's cost per tonne stays above R$3,400.
Would invalidateChinese hardwood spot falling below 4,600 RMB a tonne with Suzano conceding its November increase, or Klabin's adjusted EBITDA margin returning toward 39%.
Watch nextCopom's next decision on 9 December 2026; OKI-2's Indonesian start-up, slipped to the first quarter of 2027.
ValuationSuzano at 5.39x trailing EV/EBITDA, 1.24x book and a 9.1% free-cash-flow yield against Klabin's 6.09x, 2.15x and 2.5%; forward earnings multiples unusable.

November 28, 2026 · 3:27 AM IST

Walmart de México Added No New Shoppers Last Quarter; Its Growth Came Entirely From Price

Hypothesis Opus 5 · Research Opus 5 · Writing Opus 5 · Prompt v1.7

Mexico's formal discount shelf has stopped adding shoppers. Walmart de México's Mexican same-store sales rose 1.7% last quarter on ticket alone, with traffic flat for the first time in nine quarters and Bodega Aurrerá, the format serving its poorest households, missing its own internal plan on smaller baskets.

The money behind those baskets is shrinking: October remittances fell 1.7% year on year, a seventh straight monthly decline, and a Banco de México board member put the loss in their real peso purchasing power at more than 20% over eighteen months.

The damage is not evenly spread. Walmex operating income has fallen for three straight quarters and the shares are down 12.1% over twelve months while the Mexican index sits at a record; FEMSA's Oxxo grew same-store sales 9.2% and earns a fee paying out the remittance flow, and Banorte's bank margin came in at the high end of guidance.

Ticket grew, traffic did not

Walmart de México's Mexican same-store sales rose 1.7% in the third quarter, and all of it came from the price on the receipt. Ticket was up 1.6% and customer traffic was flat for the first time in nine quarters. The format that gave way is the one serving the lowest-income shoppers: Bodega Aurrerá, the 2,198-store discount chain, came in below Walmex's internal expectations on lower traffic and smaller shopping baskets, with weakness concentrated in larger stores in central Mexico, while Sam's Club led growth.

Mexican consumer staples are owned as the defensive corner of a market that has been working. The S&P/BMV IPC set an all-time high of 72,937 on 11 November, up about 11.3% on the year. Walmex closed at MXN53.19 on 27 November, down 12.1% over twelve months; of seventeen large Mexican listings, only the tequila maker Becle fell further. What has been marked down is the end of the shelf where the household's income arrives from abroad.

Where the basket's money comes from

Remittances to Mexico came to $5.64bn in October, down 1.7% year on year and the seventh consecutive monthly contraction. The composition matters: the number of transfers fell 5.4% while the average transfer rose 4.0% to $403, so fewer senders are sending more. Analysts in that account tie the decline to a weakening US labor market and political caution among migrants.

The 1% US excise on remittances that took effect on 1 January is the smaller force. It applies only where the sender funds a transfer with cash, a money order or a cashier's check; bank, wire, credit and debit funding are exempt, and 99.1% of January-to-October flows to Mexico arrived electronically.

The currency did the heavier work.

Banco de México's October board minutes record a member warning that the purchasing power of remittances, in pesos and net of inflation, has fallen more than 20% over eighteen months after a 10.2% appreciation, and tying that erosion to Mexican private consumption growth of just 0.8% in the first half.

It shows in the margin. Walmex operating income has fallen year on year for three straight quarters, by 2.2%, 1.4% and 0.8%, and third-quarter net income dropped 6.1% to MXN11.03bn as consolidated EBITDA margin narrowed 30 basis points to 10.2%. Guidance of 3.5% to 4.5% constant-currency sales growth was cut in April. "Consumer spending remains soft, and our performance is not yet where we want it to be," chief executive Cristian Barrientos Pozo said of a soft first quarter. On the 28 October call he described the answer: "We launched a huge campaign that called Precios que no se tocan with more than 4,000 items. We fixed the prices for more than 90 days."

Oxxo bills the flow its own shoppers live on

FEMSA reaches the same households through a different door. Oxxo Mexico same-store sales rose 9.2% last quarter, split 5.5% ticket and 3.5% traffic, and the convenience arm is also part of the country's cash plumbing: Oxxo pays remittances across more than 21,000 stores, and Spin by Oxxo, the largest banking correspondent in Mexico by regulator count, reached 11.7 million active users, up 17.3%, its loyalty program present in 52.1% of Oxxo Mexico transactions against 48.2% a year earlier. The ADR's 35.3% twelve-month gain came with compression, to 23.5x trailing earnings from roughly 46x; forward estimates of 25.5x sit above trailing, consensus saying the trailing figure, flattered by currency gains and discontinued-operations comparisons, comes down from here.

Banorte's funding cost stopped falling

The lender tests the other mechanism, and it failed. Bank net interest margin landed at the high end of guidance at 6.8%, with performing loans up 11% to MXN1.33tn, deposits up 13%, fees up 14% and return on equity of 24.5%. Nine-month profit rose 8.7% and the MXN62-64bn full-year target stands. Deposit margins are not being squeezed by an easing cycle because there barely is one: Banco de México cut to 6.25% on 5 November and signaled an extended hold. The soft spot is credit cost at 2.3% against 1.8% to 2.1% guidance, which management attributes mostly to loan growth. At 9.9x trailing earnings on 2.27x book, against about 8.8x a year ago, a little over half the 20.3% share gain is re-rating.

The month the shares moved without the numbers

Walmex gained 9.9% in the 30 days to 27 November, fifth-best among those seventeen listings, after trading below its moving averages from March to mid-October. No reported figure improved in between. Buen Fin brought more than 76 million transactions and the company's highest sales day on record on 17 November, yet fell short of Walmex's own initial expectations. The likelier reading is the currency: the peso closed at 19.71 to the dollar on 26 November, its weakest in twelve months, against 16.85 in early September, so each transferred dollar now converts into roughly a sixth more pesos than it did then.

The twelve-month de-rating was earned. Trailing earnings per share of MXN2.85 are slightly below the MXN2.91 of a year earlier, taking the trailing multiple to 18.7x from roughly 20.8x, and consensus has 2026 earnings growth at 1.5%. The November leg rests on relief that has not reached a results statement. The other two are different cases, and for a reason: Oxxo collects a fee on the inflow whatever its size, and Banorte's margin is set by a central bank that has stopped cutting.

Ahead of all three sits the wage. Proposals for 2027 were due on 30 November, with unions seeking 15% and employers about 6%; Walmex has guided to roughly 12% plus a workweek cut from 48 hours to 46, FEMSA to 13%.

That ruling lands on both sides of the Walmex ledger at once. It raises what the company pays its 240,779 employees and what the shopper who stopped walking into Bodega Aurrerá brings home, and only one of those two reaches January's income statement.

The setup

Where it standsWalmex is down 12.1% over twelve months but up about 10% in a month; FEMSA and Banorte advanced on growing earnings.
Would confirmNovember remittances below October's $5.64bn year on year, and fourth-quarter Walmex Mexico same-store sales under 3.5% with traffic negative.
Would invalidateFourth-quarter Mexico same-store sales at or above the 4.5% guidance ceiling with positive traffic and operating income up year on year.
Watch nextBanorte's extraordinary dividend vote on 1 December and Banco de México's rate decision on 17 December.

Liberty Latin America Retired a Tenth of Its Stock; Its New Preferred Yields 11.7%

The cheapest-looking equity on Latin America's carrier shelf is the one the credit market will not finance cheaply. Liberty Latin America's third-quarter revenue was $1,117m, up 0.4% year on year, with operating income down 11.7% to $181m and a net loss of $70.9m against a small profit a year earlier.

The same regional discount is landing on very different balance sheets.

Liberty Latin America sells fixed broadband, mobile and subsea capacity in Puerto Rico, Panama, Costa Rica, Jamaica and the Caribbean, and in the third quarter it sold about as much of it as a year earlier. Revenue came in at $1,117m, up 0.4% as reported and down 2% on the company's rebased basis. Operating income fell to $181m, and the net loss widened to $70.9m from a $3.3m profit.

The shares have been read as an operating turn. They are not one. Over the twelve months to 27 November the common gained 64.6% and over six months 83.2%, and over the same period the company's revenue line contracted in three of its four consumer markets: Liberty Caribbean down 1% rebased, C&W Panama down 5% on the phasing of government business projects, Puerto Rico down 3%, Costa Rica flat. What moved was the denominator.

The buyback is the growth story

More than $150m went into repurchases during 2026, concentrated in the third quarter. "We have now deployed over $150 million to date this year with a considerable portion of this in Q3, resulting in us buying back nearly 10% of our common shares outstanding as of 2025 year-end," chief executive Balan Nair told investors on 5 November. "This reflects the continued conviction that our stock trades at a meaningful discount to the intrinsic value of the business." The diluted count fell from 199.9m shares in the fourth quarter of 2025 to 194.7m in the third quarter of 2026.

That is being done against $8.5bn of total debt and consolidated net leverage of 4.5x, with $579m of cash and $860m of undrawn capacity, per the company's third-quarter release. Leverage is run silo by silo: Cable & Wireless at 3.8x with roughly five-year weighted average tenor, the Liberty Costa Rica silo below 2x, and a substantial majority of debt fixed or hedged to maturity. For comparison, América Móvil runs at 1.21x and Telefônica Brasil at 0.5x.

June's special dividend set a price on the risk

On 21 May the board committee declared a special dividend of newly issued 9.0% fixed-rate cumulative perpetual redeemable Series A preference shares, one for every ten commons, at a $25 initial liquidation price and roughly $500m in aggregate, distributed on 16 June and listed on Nasdaq. That paper closed at $19.16 on 27 November. The $2.25 annual coupon — 9.0% of the $25 face — is therefore a current yield near 11.7% on claims that rank ahead of the common.

The two lines have moved apart since the summer. The preferred has fallen 8.7% from $20.99 on 27 August while the common rose 17.2% over the same three months. The preference line is far thinner, trading between roughly 12,900 and 85,200 shares a day in November against 287,700 to 584,700 in the common, so its marks deserve that caveat. But the instrument explains the gap: one prices on yield, the other is the residual on a levered capital structure.

Price rises, not volumes, are carrying the margin

Adjusted operating income before depreciation and amortization reached $454m, up 3% rebased, at a 41% margin, 160 basis points wider. Net additions of 56,000 in postpaid mobile and broadband beat the first two quarters, including a fourth consecutive positive postpaid quarter in Puerto Rico. The mechanism is tariffs: 10% increases on fixed broadband and postpaid mobile in Jamaica, selective rises in Panama, higher video and broadband prices and fewer discounts in Puerto Rico, with more written into the 2027 budget. "So far this year, all of our price increases, we've not seen the kind of churn we've seen before in price increases," Nair said on 5 November.

Cash is improving at the margin rather than transforming. "Full year free cash flow remains on track to outperform 2025," chief financial officer Christopher Noyes said on the same call, with year-to-date adjusted free cash flow before distributions to partners running about $140m above the first nine months of 2025. Working against it: a roughly $120m year-to-date working capital headwind in Puerto Rico, vendor financing paydown, and integration and spin-off discussions with Puerto Rico debt holders on which no timing has been given.

The discount is not sorting on the fundamentals

Liberty Latin America now trades at 7.45x trailing enterprise value to EBITDA, the highest of the seven carriers on this shelf, above Millicom's 6.87x and well above América Móvil's 5.36x and TIM's 4.33x. Its 0.41x price-to-sales looks like the cheapest number in the group only because $8.5bn of debt and $500m of preference shares sit ahead of a $1.82bn equity.

The operators whose results improved most got less for it. América Móvil's quarterly revenue growth accelerated through 2026 to 6.0% in the third quarter with operating income up 16.0%, and its shares held a downtrend from 2 September to 28 October before turning up in mid-November; at 15.9x trailing and 14.95x forward earnings with a 10.1% free-cash-flow yield, that repair is the only one on the shelf matching price to operations. Telefônica Brasil grew revenue 7.2% and EBITDA 10% to a 44.5% margin and was in a downtrend from 13 November, at 4.89x EBITDA and a 9.5% free-cash-flow yield. TIM, whose EBITDA margin widened about a point to 41.3% while net income fell 18.0% as a 13.75% Selic rate taxed its financing line, was down 11.9% over twelve months at 4.33x EBITDA and a 17.2% free-cash-flow yield; its nine-month capex of BRL 3.3bn sat against BRL 20.84bn of revenue, and its dividends per share through September were BRL 0.85 against BRL 1.08 a year earlier. The Brazilian pair then gained 9.1% and 8.0% on 27 November, after Lula named Bradesco chairman Luiz Carlos Trabuco finance minister and the Ibovespa rose 6.07% — a discount-rate event, not a company one.

So almost none of Liberty Latin America's advance is explained by what it sold. A tenth fewer shares, a 160-basis-point margin gain bought with price increases, and the market's willingness to look through to a consensus that has the company losing $91m this year and earning $11.5m next — that is the move. The part the results do not cover is the part the preferred is voting on.

The company's own securities disagree about what it is worth, and the disagreement is priced to the dollar. Equity holders have paid up roughly 65% in a year for the residual; the holders of the paper in front of them want nearly 12% a year to stay. One of those two is wrong about the leverage.

The setup

Where it standsShares up 83.2% in six months on flat revenue, a widened quarterly loss, 4.5x net leverage and nearly 10% of the common retired this year.
Would confirmFull-year adjusted free cash flow above 2025 and consolidated net leverage holding at or below 4.5x while rebased revenue returns to growth.
Would invalidateRebased revenue declines deepening beyond the third quarter's 2%, or net leverage rising above 4.5x with repurchases continuing.
Watch nextFourth-quarter results, which management expects to be the year's strongest on working-capital phasing, and any timing on Puerto Rico spin-off talks with debt holders.
Valuation7.45x trailing EV/EBITDA, the highest of the seven carriers examined, against América Móvil's 5.36x and TIM's 4.33x; loss-making, so no usable earnings multiple.

Tecnoglass Set a Revenue Record and a Rising Peso Took Half Its Operating Income

Hypothesis Opus 5 · Research Opus 5 · Writing Opus 5 · Prompt v1.7

Tecnoglass bills Florida construction in dollars and pays its Barranquilla cost base in pesos, and that mismatch is what separated a record quarter from its earnings. Gross margin fell to 34.1% from 42.7% a year earlier, and management put roughly two-thirds of the decline on the currency.

The shares then rose 57.8% in the month to 27 November, the last leg of it around S&P's decision to make Tecnoglass the first Colombian company in its SmallCap 600 index, leaving them at 25.4x trailing earnings against about 14.6x a year ago.

The peso reversed hard in November, and the Colombian shelf split along currency lines: Ecopetrol's earnings grew as its shares fell with oil, Grupo Cibest's lending margin keeps rising with a policy rate held at 12.25%, and Grupo Aval's securities book is being marked against it.

Tecnoglass fabricates architectural glass and aluminium window, door and curtain-wall systems in Barranquilla, including the hurricane-resistant windows that go into Florida construction, and it sends its invoices in dollars while its factory costs accrue in Colombian pesos. In the third quarter it set a revenue record and a backlog record. Operating income fell by half.

The four Colombian large caps listed in New York have been read all year as one trade on a cheap Andean market repairing. They are not one trade. In the thirty days to 27 November Tecnoglass rose 57.8% while Ecopetrol, the state-controlled integrated oil producer, fell 23.8%, Grupo Aval 22.7% and Grupo Cibest, the holding company for Bancolombia, 10.5%. What sorts them is which currency each is paid in, set against a central bank that is not yet cutting.

A dollar invoice and a peso payroll

The official peso rate went from about 3,757 per dollar at the start of 2026 to 3,062.96 on 21 August, an appreciation of roughly 23% on the year driven by carry flows into high local rates and firm export receipts. Tecnoglass's gross margin fell to 34.1% from 42.7%, and management attributed about 580 basis points of that to a 20% year-on-year peso appreciation, 250 of it a non-cash inventory revaluation after the currency moved 12% inside ninety days. Section 232 duties cost $15.5m in the quarter, with aluminium up 52%; the US tariff on aluminium products reached 50% in June 2025 and, from 6 April 2026, is assessed on the full customs value of the imported article rather than metal content alone.

Demand was not the problem. Revenue rose 19.2% to $310.6m, multifamily and commercial work hit a record $192.4m, up 31%, and backlog reached a record $1.43bn with a book-to-bill of 1.2 times, a twenty-fourth consecutive quarter above 1.0. "Well, Florida is not doing well. It's doing extremely well. The demand is unbelievable," chief executive Jose Manuel Daes told investors on 5 November. "On the commercial side, I believe that we have work for the next five years for sure." Single-family revenue grew only 4% as reported, with US single-family starts running about 5% below the prior-year pace, and Florida slipped to roughly 75% of backlog from over 85% a year earlier.

Five sessions and an index committee

The company raised full-year revenue guidance to $1.10bn-$1.14bn and guided fourth-quarter gross margin back to 38-39% on pricing, cheaper aluminium and automation. "With a full year of pricing and incremental automation savings, we remain committed to fully offsetting the tariff impact in 2027," chief financial officer Santiago Giraldo said on the same call.

None of that has been reported yet, and the price has moved as though it had. At 25.4x trailing and 24.0x forward earnings, the shares stand against roughly 14.6x on the $3.42 of diluted earnings a year ago, while consensus 2026 earnings per share have fallen 35% to $2.47 and trailing free cash flow yield is negative 2.8%. The last stretch came in five sessions, from 47.72 on 20 November to 59.35 on 27 November, bracketing S&P's 23 November announcement that Tecnoglass replaces MarineMax in the SmallCap 600 before the 1 December open, making it the first Colombian company in the index.

The currency turned, and oil took Ecopetrol with it

In November the peso fell 12% to 3,630.89 and ended the month as the weakest currency in the world on fiscal worries, local dollar shortages and falling oil. Ecopetrol's quarter was the strongest of the four: net income rose 86% to COP 4.76tn, gross margin widened to 50.9% from 33.4%, the refining margin reached a historic $45.6 a barrel and production was 747,000 barrels of oil equivalent a day at a lifting cost of $11.4. The shares fell 24.7% from their 16 October peak as Brent, which averaged about $124 in October, retreated toward the high-$80s.

That leaves 6.57x trailing earnings, 3.97x EV/EBITDA and a 14.0% trailing free cash flow yield at 1.10x book. Consensus has 2027 earnings per share down 19%, so part of the de-rating is a forecast rather than a dislocation. The state owns 88.49% of the company, and Ecopetrol's own filings flag that the government tends to maximise dividend payouts alongside its fiscal challenges. "Market confidence is not built through announcements," new chief executive Joaquin Gutierrez said on 13 November. "It's built through consistent execution, legal certainty, and measurable results."

The two banks are on opposite sides of the same curve

Banco de la República held its policy rate at 12.25% in November, with four of seven board members voting to hold and three for another quarter-point increase; Grupo Aval expects a final 25-basis-point hike in December and cuts only from the second half of 2027. Grupo Cibest guides its 2027 net interest margin up to 7.5-7.7% on higher rates, from a record 7.4% this quarter on a COP 274tn loan book up 9.7%. Its cost of risk rises with it, to a guided 1.9-2.1% from 1.8%. "Most of the increasing cost of risk that we are expecting for 2027 comes from growth," chief strategy and financial officer Mauricio Botero Wolff said on 10 November, in commercial and consumer brackets "in which we were not participating." Third-quarter net income still fell 5.0%, at a 22% return on equity the bank itself calls rate-inflated against a 20% long-run target, and the shares carry 1.80x book against roughly 1.3x a year ago.

Aval shows the same rates from the other side. Its loan margin rose 44 basis points to 4.9%, while consolidated margin fell 191 basis points to 3.6% because the margin on its investment portfolio turned negative, at -0.1% from +8.7% a quarter earlier. Return on average equity was 7.9%, and it trades at 0.80x book.

What the quarters actually account for

Ecopetrol is the only one of the four whose twelve-month advance its earnings earn outright, and its November fall belongs to crude and to a cut in next year's estimates. The banks divide on where each one's margin sits: Cibest's inside a loan book repricing upward, Aval's inside a securities portfolio the curve has moved against. Tecnoglass is the reverse of both. Its order book and its prices are improving and its reported earnings are not, which makes the month's 57.8% a wager on a guided margin recovery plus a fixed date when index funds must own it.

Tecnoglass has told investors it is weighing a change of functional currency to the US dollar, which would end the non-cash revaluations that cost it 250 basis points of margin in the quarter. It would not move the payroll out of Barranquilla.

The setup

Subsidized Mexican Buses Are Why Volaris Could Not Pass On Its Fuel Bill and Copa Could

Hypothesis Opus 5 · Research Opus 5 · Writing Opus 5 · Prompt v1.7

Latin America's five listed carriers all bought the same dollar-priced jet fuel this year, and the share of the increase each got back from passengers ranged from about 86% at Copa Holdings to 49% at Volaris. The sorting variable is the currency the fare is written in: Copa prices dollar itineraries through Panama with only 15-20% of costs in local money, while Volaris's peso domestic fares are capped by subsidized long-distance buses and Azul's reais lost 15.6% against the dollar after Brazil's October election.

November's rally treated the group as one trade as Brent fell about 22% from its late-October peak. The business evidence splits them: Copa still earned an 18.6% operating margin and cut full-year guidance to 16-17%, Volaris beat its own EBITDA margin guidance at 25.3% on a net loss, and Azul reported record unit revenue with operating income down 32.6%. Copa's shares have re-rated to 10.0x trailing earnings from 7.4x at end-2025 while consensus 2026 earnings fell.

Jet fuel across Latin America reached about $4.61 a gallon by mid-October, 108.6% above a year earlier, taking fuel from 28% of the region's airline operating cost to 38%. What sorted the five listed carriers through that shock was not the fuel bill, which everyone pays in dollars, but the currency the fare is written in. Copa Holdings, which sells connecting itineraries through a single Panama hub where tickets are priced in dollars, recovered roughly 86% of its fuel increase last quarter. Volaris, the Mexican ultra-low-cost carrier, recovered 49%.

The market has been reading the group as one position. Brent is down about 22% from a late-October peak above $117 a barrel to $90.97 on 25 November, and in the 30 days to 27 November every one of the five rose, from LATAM Airlines at 9.5% to Volaris at 36.8%. The recapture numbers describe three different businesses, and the largest gains went to the two that passed on the least.

Dollar in, dollar out

Copa's September-quarter revenue rose 31.9% to $1.204bn, with unit revenue up 13.5% to 12.6 cents and load factor at 88.7%. Its fuel cost rose 61.5%. "Strong demand and higher yields enable us to recover approximately 86% of the increase in fuel-related expense in the quarter through higher revenues," chief financial officer Peter Donkersloot Ponce told investors on 19 November. Only 15-20% of Copa's costs sit in local currencies; the main driver of its 1.1% rise in ex-fuel unit cost was Colombian peso appreciation.

Even so, the operating margin fell to 18.6% from 23.2%, gross profit grew 9.3% on that 31.9% revenue gain, and the company cut 2026 operating-margin guidance to 16-17% on a $3.90-a-gallon fuel assumption. Net debt is 0.8x EBITDA against $1.6bn of cash. The shares now trade at 10.0x trailing and 10.3x forward earnings, against 7.4x at the end of 2025 and 6.0x at the end of 2024 — the forward figure sits above trailing because consensus 2026 earnings of $14.95 a share are 9.7% below last year's $16.28.

A bus timetable sets the Mexican fare ceiling

Volaris crossed $1bn of quarterly revenue for the first time, up 32.4%, with unit revenue up 19% to 10.31 cents and an EBITDA margin of 25.3% against its own 22% guidance. It still lost $26m.

The split inside that number is the story. Transborder US-Mexico revenue grew 53% and fully covered its fuel; peso-denominated domestic fares covered only 20-25%, because subsidized long-distance diesel buses cap what Volaris can charge Mexicans. So the airline is moving revenue into the currency its leases and fuel are in: international reaches 49% of fourth-quarter capacity, and on published fourth-quarter schedules Volaris is the largest carrier in the transborder market by seats. Grounded Pratt & Whitney-powered aircraft averaged 21 in the quarter against 41 at the start of the year, with compensation covering most fixed costs of each engine off wing but not lost revenue. The fleet still shrinks, from 154 to about 137 by end-2027, cutting lease liabilities from $3.2bn to $2.8bn.

The peso gave no help: it weakened from 18.80 to a 19.70 reference rate on 26 November, 8.8% down on the year. At 3.9x trailing EV/EBITDA and 0.26x forward sales, with consensus still modeling losses until 2028, the stock remains below its $8.88 close at end-2025. Mexico's competition authority was reported in October as set to approve the Volaris-Viva Aerobus merger before year-end.

Azul recaptured half, in a currency that fell 15%

Azul produced record unit revenue of BRL0.4723 per available seat kilometer and flat revenue of BRL5.636bn, while operating income fell 32.6% to BRL560.1m. "If you just compare our 22% with our 42% fuel RASK, that's about a 50% recapture already," president Abhi Shah said on 12 November. "Our intention is to recover 100%."

Half of a doubled dollar cost, earned in a currency that lost 15.6% after Lula's 25 October re-election, lands on BRL22.6bn of gross debt whose dollar obligations convert at R$5.18 at an average 9.9% rate. The $552m of listed equity is roughly BRL3.2bn behind that stack. The shares fell 32.6% in the 26 October session on 988,600 shares against roughly 100,000 on a typical day; American Airlines' $100m warrant exercise on 19 October moved them less than 1%. What Azul has is density — 82% of its routes carry no nonstop competitor, and loyalty, cargo and maintenance supply about 20% of unit revenue.

The spectrum holds at the top

The two larger carriers sit where the mechanism predicts. LATAM offset about 80% of a $594m quarterly fuel increase with $410m of incremental pricing and cargo revenue, guides 2026 EBITDA to $3.9-4.1bn, and trades at 10.3x forward earnings — Copa's multiple on roughly half Copa's margin. Grupo Aeroméxico recaptured 90-93% with premium cabins at 42% of revenue; its 81x forward multiple is an earnings trough, 2026 consensus of $0.22 a share rising to $1.55 in 2027.

So the durable work is the recapture, and the November prices are mostly the fuel curve. Volaris went from $5.68 on 23 October to $6.10 after its print, then to $8.68 by 11 November as crude collapsed: the quarter was worth about 7% and oil the rest. Copa's advance is a 35% multiple expansion over 2026 while its trailing earnings fell from $16.28 to $15.30 a share, with consensus assuming a 29% earnings rebound in 2027 that requires the margin squeeze to reverse. Azul's de-rating needs no explaining beyond its own balance sheet.

What none of it settles is whether the fares stay once the fuel does not. "I think it is very sticky, and we will not expect pricing to change that much if fuel comes down, especially if it comes down in a significant way," Copa chief executive Pedro Heilbron said on 19 November, noting that average fares are only about 5% above 2019 before inflation. Every dollar of that stickiness is margin for the carrier billing in dollars, and the test arrives with the next set of unit-revenue numbers.

The setup

Where it standsAll five Latin American carriers rallied with falling crude in November while their disclosed fuel recapture ranged from about 86% at Copa to 49% at Volaris.
Would confirmCopa unit revenue holding near 12.3-12.4 cents and Volaris domestic recapture rising above 25% as international capacity grows.
Would invalidateCopa fares retreating with fuel, pushing operating margin below its 16-17% guidance, or Volaris unit revenue falling back from 10.31 cents.
Watch nextMexico's competition authority decision on the Volaris-Viva Aerobus merger, reported in October as expected before year-end.
ValuationCopa 10.0x trailing and 10.3x forward earnings against 7.4x at end-2025; Volaris 3.9x trailing EV/EBITDA; Azul has no usable equity multiple.

Mexico Is Letting Its Airports Charge More Per Passenger as Fewer Passengers Arrive

Hypothesis Opus 5 · Research Opus 5 · Writing Opus 5 · Prompt v1.7

Three Mexican airport concessions stepped out of a five-month share decline in November on what looks like a traffic recovery. Their October passenger counts fell at all three, and the gain is coming from the regulated price instead.

Each group trades committed capital spending for a maximum tariff per passenger-equivalent, and each is billing a rising share of that ceiling: OMA ended the year near 93% compliance and targets 95%, GAP expects a compound increase near 7% in the first week of January. The split is in cash: OMA is cheapest at 9.63x trailing EV/EBITDA on a 6.18% free-cash-flow yield; GAP's development program leaves 2.03%; ASUR's Brazilian buying cut its EBITDA margin 7.4 points.

Mexico's aviation regulator has agreed that the country's three listed airport groups may charge more for every passenger they put through a terminal, and the next step up lands in the first days of January. In October each of the three handled fewer passengers than a year earlier.

Through November the group has been treated as a traffic story turning. The monthly counts say otherwise. At ASUR, which operates Cancún and eight other Mexican airports plus San Juan and six Colombian airports, October traffic fell 0.9% with its Mexican airports down 5.4%. GAP, twelve Mexican airports plus two in Jamaica, saw its Mexican traffic fall 7.6%, Puerto Vallarta down 19.8%. OMA, thirteen airports led by Monterrey, fell 4.8%, with Monterrey itself down 7.5%. The damage is imported: the Mexican Caribbean scheduled roughly 20% fewer US flights for summer 2026 after Spirit's May shutdown, with United cutting nearly 17% of capacity and American almost 15%.

The ceiling, and how much of it gets billed

Each group operates under a five-year Master Development Program: committed investment in exchange for a maximum tariff per workload unit, the regulated ceiling on landing, parking, jetway and security charges. The groups need not bill the whole ceiling, and how much they bill is the swing factor. "We anticipate to end this year somewhere around 93% compliance with maximum tariff. For next year, we are looking to be somewhere around 95%. We are planning to reach 100% by the third year of the five-year plan," chief executive Ricardo Dueñas said on OMA's 29 October call.

That ratchet did the work in OMA's quarter: aeronautical revenue rose 6.7% year on year and 5.3% per passenger on April's adjustment alone, with a further nominal rise "slightly above 4%" due 1 January. The uncapped book grew faster — commercial revenue up 11% to MXN 66 per passenger, VIP lounges up 28%, retail up 18.5% — and cargo, the industrial-corridor line, grew 42% on new Monterrey customers. It is the cheapest of the three at 9.63x trailing EV/EBITDA on a 6.18% trailing free-cash-flow yield, and Barclays initiated coverage at Overweight on 24 November with an MXN 300 target, citing nearshoring.

GAP needs the ratchet more, because its per-workload-unit caps edge down in December-2024 peso terms across the 2025-2029 program. "We are expecting this to increase the tariff on the first week of January in the coming year... we will have a compound increase around 7% is what we are expecting," chief executive Raul Revuelta Musalem said on 19 October, with 95% fulfilment targeted. Third-quarter EBITDA rose 19.2% to MXN 6.1bn and the margin widened 350 basis points to 67.8% on three things: the tariff, internalized technical-assistance fees, and consolidation of Cross Border Xpress, the pedestrian bridge carrying travelers from San Diego into Tijuana airport, which produced MXN 775m of revenue and MXN 558m of EBITDA in the quarter on about a million crossings. Passengers still fell 1.4%. And the cash is spoken for: MXN 8.6bn of committed capital spending in nine months leaves a 2.03% trailing free-cash-flow yield, against the dearest valuation of the three at 11.48x.

ASUR bought its way out of the regime, and paid in margin

"ASUR has evolved into the leading international airport operator across the Americas... our portfolio spans 36 airports across seven countries," chief executive Adolfo Castro said on 21 October. The CPC Aeroportos purchase closed on 1 September for BRL 5.5bn, about $992m, and took net debt to 2.6x trailing EBITDA from 0.2x. Group adjusted EBITDA margin fell 7.4 points to 60.3%, because the Brazilian assets contribute roughly 46% margins and the US commercial operations about 11%, while Mexican EBITDA fell 10%. Castro was blunt on demand: "We are not so happy of what we are seeing, and we do not know when all of this conflict in the Middle East will end and will bring a better outcome for the airlines." The shares sit at 11.37x trailing EV/EBITDA on consensus 2026 EBITDA that is 6.2% below 2025's.

The New York lines rose over the 30 days to 27 November — ASUR's ADR 9.9%, OMA 8.5%, GAP 4.0% — while the Mexico country fund EWW fell 1.7% in dollars, so this was specific to the sector. The Mexico City lines gained more, ASUR's 16.2% and GAP's 9.6%, largely on translation: the dollar-peso rate implied by the ADR-to-local ratio moved from 18.63 to 19.63 over the month, and the peso closed at 19.4242 on 24 November, its weakest since May 2025, after Banco de México cut its rate to 6.25%.

So the advance is explained by price and currency, with nothing from volume. Consensus 2026 EBITDA is flat to lower at all three — ASUR -6.2%, GAP +1.7%, OMA +0.3% — with the growth deferred to 2027 at 16.8%, 16.3% and 14.9%. November pulled that year forward. The order of who got paid follows the cash: OMA's capped tariff plus uncapped hotels, cargo and parking convert to free cash today; GAP's development program absorbs the tariff gain before it reaches shareholders; ASUR's acquisitions diluted the very margin its Mexican ceiling cannot repair, and management has disclaimed synergies.

Two decisions could settle it before February's results. Mexico's antitrust commission is expected to clear the Volaris-Viva Aerobus merger before year-end, which matters most at OMA, where the two carriers are 76% of passengers and management says it cannot yet size the effect. And the FAA's review of Mexico's civil-aviation authority identified 21 gaps to be closed by December, with a Category 2 downgrade possible as early as February 2027.

The tariff increases arrive on the calendar, in the first days of January, without reference to how many people are flying. If the US carriers that pulled out of Cancún this summer stay out, the three groups will spend next year charging more to fewer travelers, which flatters an income statement for a while and is not the same thing as growth.

The setup

Where it standsAll three groups are billing a rising share of their regulated tariff ceiling while October passenger counts fell at each of them.
Would confirmNovember and December traffic releases showing Mexican declines narrowing, and January tariff steps landing at GAP's stated ~7% compound and OMA's above-4%.
Would invalidateFurther double-digit US capacity cuts to Cancún or Puerto Vallarta, or a February 2027 Category 2 downgrade of Mexico's aviation authority.
Watch nextNovember traffic releases in early December, the antitrust ruling on Volaris-Viva before year-end, and February 2027 fourth-quarter results.

Lula's Fourth Term Cost Brazil's Banks a Fifth or More in One Session; Vale Fell 3%

Hypothesis Opus 5 · Research Opus 5 · Writing Opus 5 · Prompt v1.7

One session priced a Brazilian election, and it priced it almost entirely inside the lenders. The banks and the digital-banking platform in the iShares MSCI Brazil ETF lost between a sixth and nearly a third of their value the day after Lula's runoff win; the iron-ore exporter in the same fund lost 3.2%, and the Mexico, Peru, Chile and Colombia funds barely moved.

What was marked down was earnings in reais exposed to the federal budget and to a Selic held at 13.75%, not Latin America. Petrobras, 17.3% of the fund, reported third-quarter revenue up 40.4% and net income up 28.4% on record output, and its shares still fell 38.6% from 23 October to 25 November. Vale is the one large holding whose earnings actually deteriorated, and it fell the least of any of them.

Brazil's banks did the losing. In the first session after Lula won a fourth term with 51.8% of the runoff vote on 25 October, Itau Unibanco's American shares fell 20.4% and Bradesco's 28.0%, and the Sao Paulo exchange paused trading when the index breached a 10% circuit breaker on its worst day since 1998. Vale, the Rio de Janeiro miner that sells iron ore to Chinese steelmakers in dollars, fell 3.2%.

That asymmetry is the episode. The day was read as a country being de-rated, and the country funds obliged: the iShares MSCI Brazil ETF lost 19.8% close to close and its small-cap sibling 31.6%. But the selling landed on earnings denominated in reais and exposed to the federal budget, and it stopped at the border. That same session the Mexico fund closed up 0.05%, Peru up 0.2%, Chile down 1.2% and Colombia down 0.7%.

Two different businesses inside one wrapper

About 46% of the Brazil fund sits in five names as of 30 October: Petrobras at 17.3%, Vale 8.7%, Nu Holdings 8.5%, Itau 8.0% and the electric-motor maker WEG at 3.4%. Two of those earn dollars from commodities; two lend in local currency. Crash day sorted them accordingly. Banco do Brasil's local line fell 29.3%, Nu Holdings, the Sao Paulo digital bank with 86 million monthly active users in Brazil, fell 17.0%, and Petrobras fell 14.0%. The iShares Latin America 40 fund lost 11.2%, close to its Brazil weight multiplied by the Brazil fund's move; Petrobras, Nu, Vale and Itau are its four largest holdings as well.

Petrobras's quarter accelerated into its own selloff

The state-controlled oil group reported third-quarter revenue of $32.96bn, up 40.4% year on year, and net income of $7.74bn, up 28.4%, on production averaging 2.823m barrels of oil equivalent a day. It raised full-year operating cash flow guidance to $45-50bn from $35bn. "In the last two years alone, the production went up 3x as much as it did during 10 years," chief executive Magda Chambriard told the 11 November call.

The shares fell 38.6% between 23 October and 25 November, against 29.2% for the fund that holds them. What the market was pricing was not the quarter but the policy attached to it: fears of renewed state intervention, fuel-price controls, higher taxation and dividend risk, the levers Lula used in his third term. On the same call management confirmed fuel pricing is under internal review, with a "situational" adjustment possible by year-end and no structural change announced. Petrobras now trades at 3.5x forward earnings against 4.3x trailing, on consensus 2026 earnings of $4.80 a share, up 55% year on year, with a trailing free-cash-flow yield of 16.8%.

Vale is the counter-case, and it is the one that makes the point. Its third-quarter operating income fell 40.9% and net income 53.3% as gross margin compressed to 24.4% from 36.4%, and consensus 2026 earnings have been cut to $1.47 a share, down 27.1%. It is the only large holding whose earnings genuinely turned down, it trades at 7.0x forward earnings, and it is the holding that barely moved. A weaker real cuts its Brazilian mining costs; it does not cut the value of its iron ore.

The small-cap side travelled twice as far, both ways

The Brazil small-cap fund owns the domestic book directly: Totvs at 6.0%, the water utility Copasa at 4.9%, the grocer Sendas Distribuidora at 4.6% and Lojas Renner at 3.4%, with consumer cyclicals, real estate and utilities dominating 83 holdings. Those earnings move against the policy rate, and the central bank held the Selic at 13.75% on 4 November in a unanimous vote, ending five consecutive quarter-point cuts and citing unanchored inflation expectations.

Then the rate story reversed. Lula named Bradesco board chairman Luiz Carlos Trabuco finance minister on 26 November; the Ibovespa rose about 6.1% and long swap rates fell roughly 50 basis points. Because the US market was shut for Thanksgiving, two Brazilian sessions landed in one print: the small-cap fund gained 13.8%, the large-cap fund 10.5% and the 2x leveraged Brazil fund 20.6%. Itau rose 12.3% on 27 November; Vale rose 5.1%.

Moving-average trend measures were no help through any of it. They stayed bullish on the Brazil fund through 5 November, three weeks after the 19.8% day, and turned bearish on the Latin America 40 and leveraged funds on 18 November, two sessions before the Brazil fund's lowest close of the episode at 28.54.

Why the fund never looked cheap

The Brazil fund's trailing price-to-earnings ratio was 10.70 on 27 November, essentially where it stood in May. A drawdown of nearly a third produced no cheapening because the real went from 5.33 per dollar a year ago to 5.97 on 23 November, and a 12% devaluation cuts the dollar price and the dollar-translated local earnings together. The cheapening is specific to holdings paid in dollars.

Nor is the leverage telling anyone anything about Brazil. Over the 30 days to 25 November the 2x fund returned minus 20.4% against twice the Brazil fund's minus 20.6%, a fifth of a point of slippage. Compounding costs show up only over long windows: minus 28.0% over a year against twice minus 13.5%.

So the drawdown accounts for a policy path rather than an earnings path. The lenders and domestic small caps fell because a held Selic and a looser budget hit their revenue directly, and they recovered for the symmetrical reason when a private banker took the ministry. Petrobras fell hardest of the big names with its production and cash generation rising, which leaves its discount resting on the fuel-pricing and dividend decisions of a government that has made those decisions before.

Trabuco takes office on 5 January. Petrobras's year-end pricing review comes first.

The setup

Where it standsBrazilian funds have recovered part of the October crash after the finance-ministry appointment; the Brazil fund trades at 10.7x trailing earnings.
Would confirmPetrobras 2026 consensus earnings holding near $4.80 a share with no structural change to domestic fuel pricing or dividend policy.
Would invalidateA structural cut to Petrobras's domestic fuel prices or payout, or the Selic moving above 13.75% at a coming meeting.
Watch nextTrabuco's term at the finance ministry begins 5 January; Petrobras flagged a possible situational fuel-price adjustment by year-end.
ValuationPetrobras at 3.5x forward against 4.3x trailing earnings, a 16.8% trailing free-cash-flow yield; Vale 7.0x forward on earnings down 27%.

Originating hypothesis

category band break index composition mechanics · subject: EWZS, COLO, EWW, EWZ, ILF

The LatAm regional-ETF shelf has been marked down at genuinely gradual intensity — the ten-fund group averages -10.3% over 30 days against only -5.5% over twelve months, with not one member in any 1-month, 3-month, 6-month or 12-month mover list, yet almost every fund has stepped strongly bullish to strongly bearish across the 180- and 365-day windows (ILF, EWZS, FLN, EPU, ECH, BRZU) while two have gone the other way or barely moved (COLO is the only member in a bull band, mildly bullish over both 90 and 180 days, and EWW has repaired strongly bearish to mildly bearish inside 30 days) — and rather than another "LatAm is selling off" regional read, the question is a what-do-you-actually-own-inside-each-wrapper question told end to end: establish, holding by holding, what each fund is paid by, since EWZ is a cap-weighted bet on a handful of dollar-priced commodity exporters and big Brazilian banks, EWZS owns the domestically-geared Brazilian small caps whose earnings move inversely to the Selic and whose index is the one that broke hardest, BRZU is a daily-reset leveraged wrapper whose band flip from strongly bullish to strongly bearish in 30 days is partly compounding mechanics rather than a view on Brazil, ARGT's weight sits heavily in a Nasdaq-listed dollar earner rather than in peso assets, ECH and EPU are effectively copper-and-precious-metals funds with a pension-and-currency overlay, and COLO is a two-name oil-and-bank fund — so the same regional discount is landing on a dollar-revenue export book, a local-rate domestic book, a leverage-decay product and a commodity proxy at once.

HDFC Bank Says Its Margin Bottomed; the Fix Is an October Rate Hike That Has Yet to Land

Hypothesis Opus 5 · Research Opus 5 · Writing Opus 5 · Prompt v1.7

India's policy rate turned up in October for the first time since February 2023, and the quarter its two largest private lenders had just reported showed margins moving the wrong way. ICICI Bank's net interest margin slipped to 4.18% from 4.36% as its cost of deposits rose to 4.50%; HDFC Bank's cost of funds would not budge, because time deposits supplied most of its deposit growth.

Both banks say the repair comes from the hike itself: roughly 70% of HDFC Bank's loan book floats and reprices up by December, while term deposits reprice only at maturity. The shares moved first, on record foreign buying of Indian equities rather than on disclosed spread. Consensus has HDFC Bank's earnings growing 3.3% this fiscal year against 20.3% at ICICI, which is the whole of the gap between their multiples.

Forward fiscal years only. Blank means no analyst coverage for that year.

HDFC Bank told investors in October that its margin had reached bottom, and the thing it expects to lift that margin is the interest-rate increase the Reserve Bank of India had just delivered. The Monetary Policy Committee voted unanimously on 7 October to raise the policy repo rate 25 basis points to 5.50%, its first increase since February 2023, moving to a stance it called calibrated tightening and saying cuts were off the table in the near term. The September quarter that both of India's largest private lenders reported ten days later closed before any of that reached a loan book.

So the margins in hand went down and the margins in prospect went up, and November's rally in Indian bank shares was read as earnings confirmation. It was not that: HDFC Bank's net interest margin of 3.32% was the lowest point management identified, its reported net income grew 3.7% year on year — the weakest of the eight quarters on file — and its American depositary receipts gained a third in the month to 27 November.

A floating loan book against deposits that reprice at maturity

HDFC Bank, which gathers savings, current and term deposits across India and lends them as home, vehicle, personal and business credit, could not move its funding cost in the quarter. Cost of funds was flat at 4.4%, because time deposits supplied ₹1.3tr of the ₹1.57tr of deposit growth. Inherited borrowing maturities from HDFC Limited of roughly ₹2.6 lakh crore keep forcing that mix, holding the low-cost current and savings share down even as retail balances in those accounts grew 11.2% year on year.

The post-merger normalization of loans to deposits also stalled: deposit growth of ₹1.57tr was matched by loan growth of ₹1.58tr.

What changes is the asset side. "The 70% of floating rate book should be factored in by December [for the 25 bps rate hike], so directionally, yes, it should start improving from Q3 itself," chief financial officer Srinivasan Vaidyanathan told analysts on 17 October. Outgoing chief executive Sashidhar Jagdishan put it flatly on the same call: "The trajectory will be upward from the next quarter onwards." Asset quality gives them room — gross non-performing loans of 1.11%, down 13 basis points, with credit costs of 44 basis points and a 1.8% return on assets.

The shares now carry 16.5x trailing earnings and 2.17x book. Consensus fiscal-2027 earnings per share of ₹160.89 sits just 3.3% above the trailing four quarters' ₹155.73, so the forward multiple derived from it is about 15.9x — barely half a turn of relief for a year of waiting. The case rests on fiscal 2028, where consensus is 16.3% higher.

ICICI keeps 86 basis points more, and says where it leaked

ICICI Bank, a universal lender with 7,656 branches running deposits, mortgages, cards, insurance and wholesale banking, earned 4.18% on a comparable quarter against HDFC Bank's 3.32%. Its own compression had two named causes: overseas branches, which earn about 1% margin versus more than 4% domestically and grew as a share of the balance sheet after a foreign-currency deposit mobilization of $18bn, and retail term deposits, which pushed cost of deposits up to 4.50% from 4.41% in June, though still below 4.64% a year earlier.

"From Q4, I would expect margins to come back in a pretty healthy way as these factors start to reverse out, even assuming that there are no further rate hikes," chief financial officer Anindya Banerjee said on 17 October. Underneath, the bank delivered: pre-tax profit up 23.4%, profit after tax up 20.1% to ₹148.43bn, net interest income up 17.7%, and net non-performing loans down to 0.30% from 0.39% a year earlier. One item is unsettled — an extra standard-asset provision of ₹12.83bn on the agricultural book, pending a Reserve Bank review the company expects to resolve over the next two quarters.

At 19.3x trailing earnings, about 18.6x consensus for this fiscal year and 2.93x book, ICICI is the dearer of the two on every anchor, bought on consensus earnings growth of 20.3% this year against HDFC Bank's 3.3%.

What November actually bought

HDFC Bank's receipts rose 33.3% in the 30 days to 27 November and ICICI's 25.6%; across the year HDFC Bank is still down 21.6% while ICICI is up 16.3%. In Mumbai, HDFC Bank gained about 25% in November, its biggest monthly rise since May 2009. Foreign institutional investors bought for 16 straight sessions, a record roughly ₹1.29 lakh crore, with financial services the largest recipient and the rupee at an eight-month high. India was the biggest emerging-market recipient of those flows while South Korea and Taiwan saw heavy outflows — the same rotation that marked down Korean lenders whose own margins barely moved.

The disclosed results account for the move at one bank and not the other. ICICI's price is paying for earnings already reported and credit already improving; HDFC Bank's is paying for a spread its chief financial officer has dated to December and a year of earnings consensus still values at 3.3% growth. Jefferies, which raised its targets on 25 November to ₹1,880 for ICICI from ₹1,750 and ₹960 for HDFC Bank from ₹880, prefers ICICI first among Indian private lenders, and notes Indian equities at 2.1x one-year forward book against 2.2x for global financials after underperforming them by 46 percentage points since 2024. With HDFC Bank at ₹845.35 on 25 November, that ₹960 leaves about 13.6% — the month consumed most of the gap.

The December quarter is the first to contain the hike in full. If the loan book reprices on the two-quarter arithmetic management laid out, the margin turn arrives into a price that has already allowed for it; if the term-deposit book catches up first, HDFC Bank will have to find the earnings somewhere its own guidance has not promised them.

The setup

Where it standsIndia's repo rate is 5.50% after October's hike; both banks' September-quarter margins fell and both guide recovery from the December quarter.
Would confirmDecember-quarter net interest margin above 3.32% at HDFC Bank and above 4.18% at ICICI, with cost of deposits flat or lower.
Would invalidateMargins flat or lower again in the December quarter, or cost of deposits rising further as term deposits reprice upward.
Watch nextDecember-quarter results at both banks, and the Reserve Bank review of ICICI's ₹12.83bn agricultural provision, expected to resolve within two quarters.
ValuationHDFC Bank 16.5x trailing and about 15.9x derived fiscal-2027 earnings at 2.17x book; ICICI 19.3x trailing, about 18.6x forward, 2.93x book.

Originating hypothesis

ticker band divergence deposit funding and nim mechanics · subject: HDB, IBN, INTR

This 17-name international and emerging-market bank shelf is averaging only -3.0% over 30 days and -10.1% over twelve months — gradual, with not one member appearing in any mover list — yet underneath that quiet average the trend bands have split cleanly in two directions across the 90-, 180- and 365-day windows: every Latin American, UK, Japanese and Korean member has stepped down into mild or strong bear (AVAL, BBD, BSBR, BLX, BMA, GGAL, IFS, LYG, NWG, KB, SHG, MFG, DB), while the two Indian private banks have been repaired the other way — HDFC Bank from strongly bearish to mildly bullish across 90, 180 and 365 days, and ICICI from strongly bearish to strongly bullish over 180 and 365 days — and rather than another order-book-versus-price divergence, the question here is a mechanism question told end to end: what a deposit actually costs and what a loan actually earns at each bank when the policy rate is moving in opposite directions, since HDFC Bank is still working down a post-merger loan-to-deposit ratio by gathering low-cost CASA deposits into a falling-repo, cut-CRR environment where asset yields reprice faster than its term-deposit book, ICICI earns a structurally wider margin on a granular retail and unsecured mix funded by one of the system's cheapest deposit franchises, and Inter and Co — the one starred member here, and the one that flipped mildly bullish to strongly bearish within 30 days and strongly bullish to strongly bearish over the year — funds a fast-growing unsecured Brazilian consumer book with digital deposits priced off a Selic that has not come down, so its spread and its credit cost move against it at the same time.
